R. H. HOLLAND, 


THE FIFTEENTH 


ANNUAL REPORT 


OF THE 


Montreal Young Men's Christian Association. 


Your Committee beg to present the following Report of 
their labors and the work done by your Association during the 
past year, and in so doing they would return their humble and 
hearty thanks to God for the abundant blessings and success 
which has attended their efforts during that term, praying that the 
coming year may prove one of much spiritual and temporal pros- 
perity to the Association. 

Before proceeding to lay before you a regular , detailed state- 
ment, your Committee would draw attention to the fact that the 
Fe eee Na work of the Association has been greatl circumscribed _ 
i” “ by the increased activity on the part of the various churches of 
tea and the adoption, by them, of much of the field formerly 
joccupied by: your Association alone, and in this, also, they recog- 
cE nize the hand of God, rejoicing at these Symptoms of renewed 

vigor and energy among the people. 


MISSION COMMITTEE. 


The labors of this Committee have not been so arduous dur- 
ing the past year as in previous ones, owing, in great measure to 
the circumstance above referred to. It will be remembered that 
at the time of our last annual meeting, there was in existence a 
“ Board of City Missions,” under the direction and control of the 
pastors of the city. Desirous of avoiding anything which might, 
in any way, interfere with the labors of that Board, your Committee 
decided to withdraw entirely from the work of City Missions, and 
to continue their operations to the work among seamen and the de- 


4 


velopment of schemes in the interest of young men generally. In 
pursuance of these designs, Mr. Millen was appointed to take 
charge of the seamen’s work in summer, and to aid the members 
during the winter months, in visiting, in connexion with the Cot- 
tage Meetings. It was further intended that the Rev. C. P. Wat- 
son should labor specially among young men—he, however, having 
received and accepted a call to take the pastoral charge of a con- 
gregation in Cowansville, tendered his resignation, which was ac- 


‘ cepted, and he withdrew from the Association on the 1st of May 


last. 

Mr. Millen’s labors have been faithfully performed, as the fol- 
lowing statistics will abundantly prove : Tracts distributed, 11,049 ; 
Families and Sick visited, 1,354; visits to Public Institutions, 142 ; 
Religious Services held in the Hospital, 35, with an aggregate at- 
tendance of 425 ; Mission Prayer Meetings held, 66, attendance, 
690; Ships visited, 428 ; Bethel Services held, 28, with an atten- 
dance of 977; Families relieved, 164; Situations obtained, 3 ; 
Induced to attend Church, 1 ; Bibles given, 1. 3 

Among the incidents recorded in Mr. Millen’s diary, we find 
the following, which are selected from many others equally inte- 
resting, all combining to show that he has not labored in vain nor 
continues his self-denying labors without tokens of encouragement 
from his Divine Master. 


January 31.—Happy death of a very interesting little boy only seven 
years old. He often spoke of Jesus and of being with Jesus in heaven, and 
of going to meet his little brother and sister, and asked his father, Pa, wo’nt 
you meet me in heaven? This little child was a regular attendant upon the 
Sabbath School and was remarked by the minister for his attention. 

February 1.—Visited a family in Street, mother stupid with drink— 
father laid up with sore leg—Daughters half naked, one of them quite sick. 
The house dirty and cold with hardly any furniture. | 

March 5.—Visited a sick man, D ——, seems anxious about his soul, 
pointed him to Jesus and prayed with him. 3 

April 3.—Visited tavern in Water Street. Spoke to several soldiers and 
civilians, whom I met there, and gave them tracts ; was received very Civily. 
Visited an aged disciple who is prevented from attending our meeting through 
affliction. 

April 25.—L , a blind man who earns a scanty living by sawing 
wood, is so independent that he was two days without food rather than ask 
assistance ; a neighbor told me of him; gave him assistance. A young man 
in hospital, is very nervous ; I often call.to see him just to repeat some pre- 


5 


‘ 


cious promises and point him to Jesus. Visited one of those dens of iniquity 
on Wolfe Street; distributed tracts to the females. It makes the heart sick 
to see them, seemingly happy, on the road to ruin. May the Lord have 
mercy on them. 

May 12.—Mrs. M , in the absence of her husband, took a blanket 
from her child’s bed and sold it for drink, 

May 14.—Visited the Ship ; a young lad, H , one of the crew, 
was converted to God while in this city last season ; he still holds to the faith, 
and is highly spoken of by the men. May his example lead others to Jesus. 


June 4.—Was called at 10 P. M. to visit a dying woman. Repeated to 
her several passages of Scripture, and prayed with her; before leaving her I 
asked her if she trusted in Jesus, her only Saviour, she answered yes, and 
bowing her head, looked at me very earnestly. 

June 8.—Visited a’sick man; this person has saved up all the tracts 
which have been given him, and has sent them round the country after read- 
ing them himself, hoping to benefit others in this way. 


August 7.—Visited Mrs. , drinks and neglects her children; her 
house filthy and untidy. Blames every one but herself for her troubles. 

Held religious service in the Hospital. After service an aged woman 
thanked me kindly for my advice. 

September 25.—Visited seventeen families. Met with an old Sabbath 
school scholar, now the father of a family—he was under the influence of 
liquor, and tried to sing some hymns, and repeated several passages of Scrip- 
ture. Several of the poor people blessed me heartily as_I left their door. 
Lord, teach these erring ones the way of salvation. 


October 11.—Visited fourteen families; seem to have very little comfort 
in this world and will not be persuaded to take God’s word for their guide to 
a better world. An aged man asked me to read and explain the 7th chapter of 
Hebrews to him ; did so, and called his particular attention to the 25th verse. 


The Cottage Meeting work was not prosecuted with the zeal 
and earnestness of previous years. From four districts only out 
of the thirteen, into which the city is divided, have your Commit- 
tee received reports with any degree of regularity, in these, meet- 
ings were held twice in each week, the average attendance being 
about twelve. That they have proved a blessing to those who at- 
tended them, and that the good report of them is gone abroad, is 
manifested from the: fact that the re-opening of them is anxiously 
desired, and a request has already been sent in from a needy dis- 
trict earnestly intreating that it may also be included among the 
fields of labor now occupied by the young men of this Association ; 
truly, this is a call, “come over and help us,’ ’ who can withold a 
ready and willing response, such as that of the prophet, “ Here 
am. I, send me.” , 


sigan 
wy 


6 


TRACT DISTRIBUTION. 


This branch of our work sustained a severe loss by the sud- 
den death of its devoted chairman, Mr. R. Kneeshaw, who for 
about four years had most efficiently directed and controlled it. 
Mr. T. C. Jones was appointed his successor, and has, up to the 
present time, ably performed the duties connected with the office. 
The wharves, were, as usual, divided into districts, each of which 
has been regularly visited from Sabbath to Sabbath by those vol- 
unteering for the work. 40,000 pages of tracts have been distri- 
buted, 400 visits have been made to sea-going vessels, and 300 to 
river craft. Inthe course of conversation with the sailors much 
encouragement has been given and received, which those engaged 
in the work can look back upon with feelings of joy and satisfac- 
tion scarcely to be appreciated by others. May God bless them 
and increase their number and efficiency. 


MEMBERSHIP, ROOMS AND LIBRARY. 


The roll of Members has been increased by 7o during the 
year, and now numbers 400. Some have left for other cities, 
taking with them letters of introduction to other Associations, and 
a few have withdrawn their names, assigning, as reasons, their in- 
ability, owing to other engagements of attending the meetings or 
visiting the rooms. Your Committee recommend that the roll be 
now thoroughly revised and corrected. | 

Not long after your Committee came into office, their atten- 
tion was directed to the fact that the expenditure far exceeded the 
income of the Association, so much so, that they deemed it their 
duty to retrench as much as possible. The rooms, then in use, 
cost in rent and taxes about $600, and the Room Committee were 
instructed to obtain, if possible, suitable rooms at less expense. 
These, at present occupied, were subsequently chosen at a rental 
of only $200 annually, free of taxes, a direct saving of about $400 ; 
and it is pleasing to note that the misgivings of many, as to the 
locality of your new rooms, have been entirely unnecessary, the 
result proving more satisfactory than could have been anticipated, 
as a greater number of young men have visited the rooms since 
their removal than at any previous time of equal duration. The 


expense of moving and fitting up was very small, the only item 


7 


being the removal of partitions which were in the new rooms. The 
material and labor for decorating were furnished by a few mem- 
bers of the Association. 

The Reading Room is very well supplied with reading matter, 
which it is hoped will be greatly added to during the coming year. 
We are now in receipt of 7 illustrated papers, 4 daily, 1 try-weekly, 
and six weekly commercial, and 1o religious papers, also, 51 
pamphlets and periodicals exclusive of such publications as are 
occasionally given by friends. The greater part of the periodicals 
received regularly are obtained through the generosity of friends 
taking them, who kindly permit them to remain for a week or a 
month in the rooms (i. e. until the next number comes,) before 
taking them home. 

The Library is being well used, at present the Librarian has 
276 names of members on the roll of those making use of the 
books. ‘The valuable reference works are becoming more appre- 
ciated, and it is hoped that the number of those consulting them 
will be much increased as their value and facility of access be- 
come more widely known. ‘The value and completeness of that 
portion of the Library having reference to Sabbath School labor 
has been specially remarked, and as this Library is free to all Sab- 
bath School teachers of the city, it is desirable that more of those | 
should make use of the works. 

A few volumes have been presented to the library during the 
year. 


LECTURES, CLASSES AND MEETINGS. 


A course of lectures was delivered by Dr. Dawson, last win- 
ter, in aid of the funds of the Association ; these were eminently 
successful, and a considerable sum was realized which aided very 
materially to lessen our financial difficulties. 

It is intended, if at all possible, to secure the services of our 
city pastors and others in addressing the members in the rooms at 
least once in each month, and, should this project be carried out, 
it is hoped that the members will avail themselves of the oppor- 
tunities, thus afforded, of manifesting their interest in the under- 
taking. 

The Literary Class which had been organized under the.able 
supervision of the Rev. C. P. Watson, continued to hold its regu- 


% 


lar weekly meetings until the 25th of May, when it adjourned 


until the sth of October last. Mr. Watson having left the city, © | 


the members unanimously agreed to request the Rev. Dr. Hamil- 
ton to become their president, this request he willingly acceded to, 
and has since continued ably to discharge the duties of that office. 
The roll of members numbers at present 74, with an average at- 
tendance of 26. Since our last annual meeting they have held 30 
meetings, at which were 21 readings, 18 recitations, 9 discussions, 
9 essays, and 8 debates. 

The Office Bearers at present are: Rev. Dr. Hamilton, presi- : 
dent ; Messrs. Cushing and McLaren, vice-presidents ; Mr. R. H. 
Holland, secretary ; and Messrs. Jones, Middlemiss and Fitts, 
committee. : 

An exceedingly interesting Bible Class was organized on Sun- 
day the 23rd September last under the leadership of Dr. Dawson ; 
no less than 150 were present at its opening, not a few of whom 
were ladies. Last Sunday 120 were present, and this has been 
the average attendance for some time past, and by far the larger 
portion are Sabbath School teachers. The subject chosen for 
discussion during the winter months is “some aspects of the Life 
and Teachings of our Lord Jesus Cerist, as recorded in the Gos- 
pels.” In the course thus far pursued, John’s Testimony to Christ, 
the Miracle at Cana of Galilee, and the Visit of Nicodemus to 
Christ, have been incidents under consideration, and all the meet- 
ings have proved deeply interesting. 

The idea of a French Class in the rooms has been frequently 
before your Committee, and they have at last secured the services 
of a competent teacher. As soon, therefore, as a sufficient num- 
ber have signified their intention to join, the class will be estab- 
lished ; the charges are to be merely sufficient to meet the neces- 
sary expenses. 

The regular Tuesday evening meetings of the Association have 
been well sustained throughout the year with a marked increase 
of earnestness as well as numbers. One precious soul, at least, 
has been awakened and turned to God through their instrumental- 
ity. How many more of which your Committee can have no 
knowledge, the last great day alone will reveal. ‘That they have 
proved a blessing to all who attended them is abundantly testified. 

Social meetings have been held in the rooms about once a 


v 


month, proving of great value in rendering the members acquainted 
with one another, and tending to promote good will and fellowship. 

In accordance with a resolution passed at the Annual Con- 
vention of Young Men’s Christian Associations of the United 
States and British Provinces held last June, in Albany, your Com- 
mittee issued a circular to the clergymen of the city, requesting 
them, on the first Lord’s day in November, to lay before their 
congregations, and especially young men, the objects and claims 
of the Young Men’s Christian Associations. Your Committee 
was highly gratified with the almost unanimous response which 
this request elicited. In most of the Protestant churches of the 
city discourses were addressed specially to young men, and the 
claims of the Association fairly presented. 

In accordance with the same resolution, a special meeting 
was. held on the Saturday evening previous, the object being 
united prayer for the increase and spiritual prosperity of Young 
Men’s Christian Associations throughout the world. The meeting 
was well’ attended ; a deep feeling of earnestness prevailed, and 
all present experienced, the fulfilment of the promise, that where 
two or three are gathered together in the name of the Lord, He is 
in the midst of them. 

The Convention above referred to was the Eleventh Annual 
Meeting of the kind. Your Association was represented there by 
Rev. Geo. Douglas, Messrs. D. Bentley, T. J. Claxton, E. 8. Ly- 
man, C. C. Macdougall, and A. Sandham. All its meetings were 
characterized by an unusual degree of spirituality, unity and bro- 
therly love. Your delegates met with a most cordial and hearty 
reception, and their invitation to the Associations to hold their 
next Convention in Montreal was unanimously accepted. Great 
responsibility, therefore, will devolve upon your incoming Commit- 
tee, that suitable preparation, be made for the reception of our 
brethren, and it is earnestly hoped that each member of the Asso- 
ciation will feel that he has something to do in this matter, in seek- 
ing, meantime, the spiritual good of our own Association, that its 
influence over those visiting us may be greatly blessed. 


SPECIAL WORK. 


There is a constant influx to our city, both from the country 
parts and towns of these Provinces, and from other and distant 
B 


IO 


countries of young men seeking situations : their temptations are 
ereat—their wants many. ‘To aid and benefit these is one of the 
great objects of this Association, and in endeavoring to fulfil it 
your Committee caused notices, neatly framed, to be hung up in 
all the principal hotels of the city, and on all steamers regularly 
carrying passengers to this port, giving the name and address of 
the Association and a free invitation and urgent request to all 
strangers to visit it. Your secretary, Mr. Sandham, has been in 
constant attendance to supply the wants of such as came as far as 
he was able ; the result has been that situations have been obtained 
for 31; boarding houses for 46; 2 have been induced to attend 
church ; 16 letters of introduction have been given to other Asso- 
ciations ; while $32.50 have been expended in aiding those who 
were in distress, and were found, after close enquiry, to be deserv- 
ing of such aid. 

During the Fenian raids your president offered the services 
of 20 young men to aid the Citizen’s Relief Committee in deliver- 
ing parcels at the various camps, on the understanding that these 
should also act in the capacity of a Christian commission. The 
offer was accepted, and during the week or ten days that the vol- 
unteers were on duty, each camp was visited, and in addition to 
the aid rendered to the Relief Committee, your delegates distri- 
buted over 1,000 copies of “The British Workman,” 1,000 of the 
“Band of Hope,” 9,000 pages of tracts, 75 small copies of “ Pil- 
erim’s Progress,” and 300 small books and pamphlets. Prayer 
meetings were held in the camps whereever practicable, and the 
reports of the delegates show that every assistance, in their power, 
was rendered them by the officers. 

The first visit was made to the camps at St. Johns and St. Armands. 
At these camps the delegates were greatly assisted by the kindness of Cols. 
Pipon and Fane who furnished any passes which might be necessary, and in 
other ways aided them in their labors. The men gladly received the tracts 
and papers, and when it was known in the camp that they were being distri- 
buted, the men might be seen running after the delegates and requesting that 
they might also have some. Some of the men were very earnest in their 
thanks, and the brethren, who visited these camps, report that they felt 
themselves amply repaid for any inconvenience they may have experi- 
enced. The subsequent visits to the camps at these places were equally 
interesting. 

At the camps at Huntingdon and Durham, religious services were held 
in the church and barrack-room, and were well attended; the men listened | 


II 


with deep attention,to the remarks made and joined heartily in the singing. 
Lt.-Col. O. Smith and Major Stevenson rendered valuable services to the 
delegates and attended the meetings which were held. 

At the camp of the Royals, at Hemmingford, a prayer-meeting was organ- 
ized in one of the tents, which, we are pleased to say, was kept up, by some 
of the men, as long as the camp remained at that place. 

The Committee also made up small packages of bound volumes, which 
they forwarded to camp for use among the men. 

Our thanks are due to the following gentlemen for kind donations of 
reading matter for the volunteers: T. J. Claxton, Esq., three large bundles 
containing, each, an assortment of British Workman, Band of Hope, Tracts, 
small edition of Pilgrim’s Progress, with other works, also 400 copies.Good 
Words, and 200 copies Sunday Magazine. John Lovell, Esq., 36 bound vol- 
umes and 12 pamphlets. Professor Dawson, 6 Leisure Hour and 49 miscel- 
laneous works. Dawson Bros., 24 Sunday at Home, 39 Good Words, 16 
Family Treasury, and 43 pamphlets. Miss McDonald, 120 copies New York 
Witness, and 50 Way-Marks in the Wilderness. Also, from the Proprietors 
Montreal Gazette; Herald and Witness for a donation of papers—daily. : 


Such is a brief summary of the year’s labor. Much has been 
performed which the limits of this brief report necessarily exclude ; 
much—very much remains to be done, and your Committee, before 
retiring, beg to urge all to increased activity. ‘“ What thy hand 
findeth to do, do it with thy might,” “work while it is called to- 
day.” Four of our members have been suddenly removed from 
our midst by the hand of death, three of them with scarcely a 
moment’s warning ; “be ye also ready,” that when the Master calls 
you may be able to answer, “I have finished the work which thou 
gavest me to do.” 

The whole respectfully submitted.

[ONSTITUTION, 


ARTICLE I. 


This Society shall be called ‘“‘ THE MONTREAL YounG MEN’s CHRIS- 
TIAN ASSOCIATION.” 


ARTICLE II. 


Its objects shall be, the ve/zgzows and mental improvement of its Mem- 
bers, especially in connection with the study of the Scriptures; the union of 
young men of various Churches in this and other plans of usefulness ; and 
the providing of means by which young men, coming as strangers into the 
city, may be brought under religious influences among their own class. 


ARTICLE III. 


This Association adopts, as the basis of all its proceedings, those fun- 
damental principles of Evangelical Christianity on which all Orthodox Pro- 
testant Churches are agreed, and will never admit any intermeddling with 
those matters of Faith and Polity on which such Churches differ. 


ARTICLE IV. 


This Association shall be composed of Active, Associate, Life, and 
Honorary Members. Any young man, who is a member in good standing of 
an Evangelical Church in this city, may be elected an Active Member. Any 
young man, of good moral character, may be elected an Associate Member. 
Any Associate Member, who shall unite with an Evangelical Church, becomes 
thereby an Active Member, due notice thereof having been given to the Sec- 
retary. Any member in good standing of an Evangelical Church, who con- 
tributes $100 to the funds of the Association at one time, may be elected a 
Life Member. An Active Member, by contributing $100 to the funds at one 
time, thereby becomes a Life Member. Active, Life, and Honorary Members 
only have the right to vote, and be eligible to office. The Association shall 
have power to expel members. 


ARTICLE V. 

The annual subscription for Active and Associate Members shall be 
One Dollar, payable in advance. 

ARTICLE VI. 

The Officers of the Association shall be—a President, four Vice-Prest- 
dents, a Treasurer, and a Secretary ; these, with Fifteen members of Com- 
mittee, shall form the General Committee of the Association. 

ARTICLE VIL. 

An Annual Meeting shall be held in the month of November, to re- 

ceive the Report of the General Committee and elect their successors. 
ARTICLE VIII. i 
All elections shall be by ballot. 


14 


ARTICLE IX. 


All meetings of the Association and Committee shall be opened and 
closed with prayer. Seven members shall be a quorum of the Association, 
and five of the General Committee. 


ARTICLE X. 


It shall be competent for the General Committee, with the approval of 
the Association, to engage such persons as may be deemed necessary to 
carry out the objects of the Association. 


ARTICLE XI. 


This Constitution shall not be altered or amended except by a two- 
thirds vote of the members present at the Annual Meeting, or at a Special 
Meeting called for that purpose. A month’s notice of any proposed altera- 
tion or amendment must be given to the Association. 


PY-LAws. 


ARTICLE I.—MEMBERSHIP. 


1.—All propositions for membership shall be made in writing by an 
Active Member, at a regular meeting of the Association, and shall contain the 
name in full, the residence, the church of which the candidate is a member, 
or if not a church-member, the congregation with which he is connected, and 
shall be signed by the proposer. Elections shall not take place before the 
next succeeding business meeting. 
2.—The Members shall seek out young men taking up their residence 
in the city, endeavour to bring them under moral and religious influences, and, 
by every means in their power, to surround them with Christian associates. 
Members shall also exert themselves to interest the churches to which they 
respectively belong in the objects and welfare of the Association. They shall 
jabour to induce all suitable young men of their acquaintance to connect them- 
selves with the Association, and use all practicable means for increasing its 
membership, activity and usefulness. 


ARTICLE I].—DvutTIES OF OFFICERS. 


r.—It shall be the duty of the President, or in his absence, of a Vice- 
President to preside at all meetings of the Association and General Committee, 
and to preserve in strict exercise the rules established by Parliamentary order. 

>.—It shall be the duty of the Treasurer to receive all monies, and to 
disburse the same under the direction of the General Committee. He shall 
keep a full and correct account of his transactions, and report to the General 
Committee when so required, and to the Association at its Annual Meeting. 

3.—It shall be the duty of the Secretary to keep a correct record of the 
proceedings of all meetings of the Association, and of the General Committee ; 
to keep a full and complete register of the. name, residence, and church of 
each member ; to notify all Officers and Members of their election or appoint- 
ments ; and to prepare the work for the business meetings. He shail, under 
the direction of the General Committee, conduct the correspondence of the 
Association, and keep copies of all letters written, and fyles of those received. 
He shall also prepare the Annual Report of the General Committee. 

—The General Committee shall have the management of the affairs 

of the Association, and shall present a report at each monthly business meet- 
;ng, and at the annual meeting. 


ARTICLE III.—STANDING COMMITTEES. 


1.—From the Genefal Committee the President shall appoint the fol- 
lowing Standing Committees :—A Committee on Membership, Rooms and 
Library ; a Committee on Missions ; a Committee on Lectures, Classes and 
Meetings ; a Committee on Finance ; and a Committee on Boarding-houses. 
They shall report to each monthly meeting of the General Committee. The 
President and Secretary shall be ex-officio members of each Standing Com- 
mittee. 

2.—The Committee on Membership, Rooms and Library, shall consist 
of five members, to whom all propositions for membership shall be referred. 


16 


They shall secure the co-operation of an active member in each Evangelical 
Church in the city, who shall report upon propositions referred to him, seek out 


- new members, and endeavour to interest his congregation in the Association. 


They shall also take charge of the Rooms and Library of the Association. 

3.—The Committee on Missions shall: consist of five members, and it 
shall be their duty to superintend the Mission work of the Association. 

4.—The Committee on Lectures, Classes and Mectings, shall consist of 
five members, and shall provide for the delivery of Lectures or Sermons ; 
have charge of Bible and Literary Classes, and all meetings not under the 
direction of the Committee on Missions. 

s.—The Committee on Finance shall consist of three members, shall 
devise means for obtaining necessary funds for the Association ; and shall 
examine and approve all accounts referred to them by the General Committee 
previous to their payment by the Treasurer. The Treasurer shall be an ex- 
officio member of this Committee. 

6.—The Committee on Boarding-houses shall consist of three members, 
and it shall be their duty to aid young men in finding suitable boarding-houses, 
and to endeavour to establish family worship in such places where it is not 
observed. ,. 


ARTICLE IV.—ELECTION OF GENERAL COMMITTEE. 


1.—At the last business meeting previous to the Annual Meeting, the 
General Committee shall nominate its successors, and other nominations shall 
then be received. | 

2.—A majority of the votes cast shall be an election. | 

3.—Any member of the General Committee absenting himself from 
three consecutive monthly meetings of the Committee, without sufficient rea- 
son, shall vacate his office. All vacancies shall be filled by the General 
Committee. 


ARTICLE V.—MEETINGS. 


\ 


1.—A Regular Meeting of the Association shall be held every Tuesday 
evening. A business Meeting shall be held oh the Second Tuesday of each 
month. 1d 
2,—The General Committee shall meet each month previous to the 
regular business meeting of the Association. ; 

3.—Special meetings of the General Committee may be called at the 
option of the President, or at the request of three Members of the Committee. 
Special Meetings of the Association shall be held at the written request of 
ten members, or at the option of the President, to be called by public ad- 
vertisement. 


6 
ARTICLE VI.—ALTERATIONS. 


1.—No alterations or additions shall be made to these By-Laws, except 
by a two-thirds vote of the members present at a business meeting. A month’s 
notice of the proposed change shall be given to the Association. 

2.—Any By-Law may be suspended for the time being bya two-thirds 
vote of the members present at a business mecting.
